title: III. The Second Marriage And The Second Family
section: Book I — The History Of A Family
paragraphs: Very soon after getting his four-year-old Mitya off his hands, Fyodor Pavlovitch married a second time. His second marriage lasted eight years. He took this second wife, Sofya Ivanovna, also a very young girl, from another province, where he had gone on some small bit of business in the company of a Jew. Though Fyodor Pavlovitch was a drunkard and a vicious debauchee, he never neglected to invest his capital, and managed his business affairs very successfully—though, no doubt, not especially scrupulously. Sofya Ivanovna was the daughter of an obscure deacon, and had been left an orphan from childhood, with no relatives. She grew up in the house of a general's widow, a wealthy old lady of good position, who was at once her benefactress and her tormentor. I don't know the details, but I've heard that the orphan girl, a meek and gentle creature, was once cut down from a halter in which she was hanging from a nail in the loft—so terrible were her sufferings from the whims and endless nagging of this old woman, who apparently wasn't bad-hearted, but had become an insufferable tyrant through sheer idleness.

Fyodor Pavlovitch made her an offer; inquiries were made about him, and he was refused. But again, as in his first marriage, he proposed an elopement to the orphan girl. There's very little doubt she would never have married him under any circumstances if she'd known a little more about him in time. But she lived in another province; besides, what could a little girl of sixteen know about it, except that she would be better off at the bottom of the river than remaining with her benefactress? And so the poor child exchanged a benefactress for a benefactor. This time Fyodor Pavlovitch did not get a penny, because the general's widow was furious. She gave them nothing and cursed them both. But he had not been counting on a dowry; what lured him was the remarkable beauty of the innocent girl, above all her innocent appearance, which had a peculiar attraction for a vicious profligate who until then had admired only the coarser types of feminine beauty.

"Those innocent eyes slit my soul up like a razor," he used to say afterwards, with his loathsome snigger. In a man so depraved this might, of course, mean no more than sensual attraction. Since he had received no dowry with his wife, and had, so to speak, taken her "from the halter," he didn't stand on ceremony with her. Making her feel that she had "wronged" him, he took advantage of her phenomenal meekness and submissiveness to trample on the elementary decencies of marriage. He gathered loose women into his house and carried on orgies of debauchery in his wife's presence. To show how bad things had become, I should mention that Grigory—the gloomy, dim, stubborn, argumentative servant who had always hated his first mistress, Adelaïda Ivanovna—took the side of his new mistress. He championed her cause, abusing Fyodor Pavlovitch in a manner hardly befitting a servant, and on one occasion broke up the revels and drove all the disorderly women out of the house. In the end this unhappy young woman, kept in terror from her childhood, fell into that kind of nervous disease most often found in peasant women who are said to be "possessed by devils." At times, after terrible fits of hysterics, she even lost her reason. Yet she bore Fyodor Pavlovitch two sons, Ivan and Alexey, the eldest in the first year of marriage and the second three years later. When she died, little Alexey was in his fourth year, and, strange as it seems, I know that he remembered his mother all his life—like a dream, of course. At her death, almost exactly the same thing happened to the two little boys as had happened to their elder brother, Mitya. They were completely forgotten and abandoned by their father. They were looked after by the same Grigory and lived in his cottage, where they were found by the tyrannical old lady who had raised their mother. She was still alive and had not, in all those eight years, forgotten the insult done to her. All that time she had been obtaining exact information about her Sofya's way of life, and, hearing of her illness and hideous surroundings, she declared aloud two or three times to her servants:
"It serves her right. God has punished her for her ingratitude."

Exactly three months after Sofya Ivanovna's death, the general's widow suddenly appeared in our town, and went straight to Fyodor Pavlovitch's house. She spent only half an hour in town, but she accomplished a great deal. It was evening. Fyodor Pavlovitch, whom she had not seen for those eight years, came in to her drunk. The story goes that the instant she saw him, without any sort of explanation, she gave him two good, ringing slaps on the face, seized him by a tuft of hair, and shook him three times up and down. Then, without a word, she went straight to the cottage where the two boys were. Seeing at a glance that they were unwashed and in dirty linen, she promptly gave Grigory, too, a box on the ear, and announcing that she was taking both children away, she wrapped them up just as they were in a rug, put them in the carriage, and drove off to her own town. Grigory accepted the blow like a devoted slave, without a word, and when he escorted the old lady to her carriage, he made her a low bow and pronounced impressively that "God would repay her for the orphans." "You're a blockhead all the same," the old lady shouted at him as she drove away.

Fyodor Pavlovitch, thinking it over, decided it was just as well, and did not refuse the general's widow his formal consent to any arrangement regarding his children's education. As for the slaps she had given him, he drove all over town telling the story.

It so happened that the old lady died soon after this, but she left the boys a thousand roubles each in her will "for their instruction, and so that all be spent on them exclusively, with the condition that it be so apportioned as to last till they are twenty-one, for it is more than adequate provision for such children. If other people think fit to throw away their money, let them." I haven't read the will myself, but I hear there was something odd of the sort, whimsically worded. The principal heir, Yefim Petrovitch Polenov, the Marshal of Nobility of the province, turned out, however, to be an honest man. Writing to Fyodor Pavlovitch, and realizing at once that he could extract nothing from him for his children's education (though the latter never refused outright, but only procrastinated, as he always did in such cases, and was, in fact, at times effusively sentimental), Yefim Petrovitch took a personal interest in the orphans. He became especially fond of the younger, Alexey, who lived for a long time as one of his family. I beg the reader to note this from the start. And to Yefim Petrovitch, a man of a generosity and humanity rarely to be met with, the young men owed their education and upbringing more than to anyone else. He kept the two thousand roubles left to them by the general's widow intact, so that by the time they came of age their portions had been doubled by accumulated interest. He educated both of them at his own expense, and certainly spent far more than a thousand roubles on each of them. I won't go into a detailed account of their boyhood and youth, and will mention only a few of the most important events. Of the elder, Ivan, I will only say that he grew up into a somewhat morose and reserved, though far from timid, boy. By the age of ten he had realized that they were living not in their own home but on other people's charity, and that their father was a man of whom it was disgraceful to speak. This boy began very early, almost in his infancy (so they say at least), to show a brilliant and unusual aptitude for learning. I don't know exactly why, but he left the family of Yefim Petrovitch when he was barely thirteen, entering a Moscow gymnasium and boarding with an experienced and celebrated teacher, an old friend of Yefim Petrovitch. Ivan used to say afterwards that this was all due to the "zeal for good works" of Yefim Petrovitch, who was captivated by the idea that the boy's genius should be trained by a teacher of genius. But neither Yefim Petrovitch nor this teacher was living when the young man finished at the gymnasium and entered the university. Since Yefim Petrovitch had made no provision for the payment of the tyrannical old lady's legacy, which had grown from one thousand to two, it was delayed, owing to the formalities inevitable in Russia, and the young man was in serious straits for his first two years at the university, since he was forced to support himself the whole time he was studying. It must be noted that he didn't even try to communicate with his father, perhaps out of pride, out of contempt for him, or perhaps out of his cool common sense, which told him that from such a father he would get no real help. However that may be, the young man was by no means discouraged and managed to find work, at first giving cheap lessons and later getting paragraphs on street incidents published in the newspapers under the signature of "Eye-Witness." These paragraphs, it was said, were so interesting and piquant that they were soon snapped up. This alone showed the young man's practical and intellectual superiority over the masses of needy, unfortunate students of both sexes who hang around the offices of the newspapers and journals, unable to think of anything better than endless entreaties for copying and translations from the French. Having once made contact with the editors, Ivan Fyodorovitch always kept up his connection with them, and in his later years at the university he published brilliant reviews of books on various specialized subjects, so that he became well known in literary circles. But only in his last year did he suddenly manage to attract the attention of a far wider circle of readers, so that a great many people noticed and remembered him. It was a rather curious incident. When he had just left the university and was preparing to go abroad on his two thousand roubles, Ivan Fyodorovitch published in one of the more important journals a strange article that attracted general notice, on a subject of which he might have been supposed to know nothing, since he was a student of natural science. The article dealt with a subject that was being debated everywhere at the time—the status of the ecclesiastical courts. After discussing several opinions on the subject, he went on to explain his own view. What was most striking about the article was its tone, and its unexpected conclusion. Many of the Church party regarded him unquestioningly as on their side. And yet not only the secularists but even the atheists joined in the applause. Finally, some shrewd persons concluded that the article was nothing but an impudent, satirical burlesque. I mention this incident particularly because this article reached the famous monastery in our neighborhood, where the inmates, being particularly interested in the question of the ecclesiastical courts, were completely bewildered by it. Learning the author's name, they took an interest in the fact that he was a native of the town and the son of "that Fyodor Pavlovitch." And just then the author himself made his appearance among us.

Why Ivan Fyodorovitch had come among us, I remember asking myself at the time with a certain uneasiness. This fateful visit, which was the first step leading to so many consequences, I never fully explained to myself. It seemed strange on the face of it that a young man so learned, so proud, and apparently so cautious, should suddenly visit such an infamous house and a father who had ignored him all his life, hardly knew him, never thought of him, and would under no circumstances have given him money, though he always feared that his sons Ivan and Alexey would also come to ask him for it. And here the young man was staying in the house of such a father, had been living with him for two months, and they were on the best possible terms. This last fact was a particular cause of wonder to many others besides me. Pyotr Alexandrovitch Miüsov, of whom we've already spoken, the cousin of Fyodor Pavlovitch's first wife, happened to be in the neighborhood again on a visit to his estate. He had come from Paris, which was his permanent home. I remember he was more surprised than anyone when he made the young man's acquaintance, who interested him extremely, and with whom he sometimes argued and, not without an inner pang, compared himself in accomplishments.

"He is proud," he used to say, "he'll never be short of money; he has enough to go abroad right now. What does he want here? Everyone can see he hasn't come for money, since his father would never give him any. He has no taste for drink and dissipation, and yet his father can't do without him. They get on so well together!"

That was the truth; the young man had an unmistakable influence over his father, who actually seemed to be behaving more decently and even appeared at times ready to obey his son, though he was often extremely, even spitefully, perverse.

It was only later that we learned that Ivan had come partly at the request of, and in the interests of, his elder brother, Dmitri, whom he saw for the first time on this very visit, although before leaving Moscow he had been in correspondence with him about an important matter of more concern to Dmitri than to himself. What that business was the reader will learn fully in due course. Yet even when I knew of this special circumstance, I still felt Ivan Fyodorovitch to be an enigmatic figure, and thought his visit rather mysterious.

I should add that Ivan appeared at the time in the role of a mediator between his father and his elder brother Dmitri, who was in open quarrel with his father and was even planning to bring an action against him.

The family, I repeat, was now united for the first time, and some of its members were meeting for the first time in their lives. The younger brother, Alexey, had already been among us for a year, having been the first of the three to arrive. It is of that brother Alexey that I find it most difficult to speak in this introduction. Yet I must give some preliminary account of him, if only to explain one odd fact—namely, that I have to introduce my hero to the reader wearing the cassock of a novice. Yes, for the last year he had been in our monastery, and seemed willing to be cloistered there for the rest of his life.
